title: Flower festival
hook: Hanamatsuri in Japan: flowers and sweet tea for the baby Buddha

segments.voice: Yesterday, a third Vesak, and the Buddha's words to Ananda: be lamps unto yourselves. Your line: the third lamp. Did you sit with one light? Day one thousand fifty-four.

You've stood in this courtyard before. In your first year on this path, Hanamatsuri arrived as a new word: a tiny roofed shrine covered in fresh flowers, a little statue of the baby Buddha, one hand pointing up and one pointing down, and a line of children ladling sweet tea over his head. The flowers and the tea come back every spring. This time, look past the scene to the old text behind it, and to the quiet turn at its very end, which is easy to miss.
screen: `THE FLOWER SHRINE, AGAIN.` → `ONE HAND UP, ONE HAND DOWN.` → `A QUIET TURN IN AN OLD TEXT.`

segments.voice: The birth story the festival acts out comes from a sutta in the Majjhima Nikaya, the one on wonderful and marvelous qualities. Its setting is easy to skip. Monks are sitting together after their meal, marveling at the Buddha's powers, when he walks in and asks what they were talking about. He asks Ananda to say more, and Ananda recites a long list of wonders he says he heard from the Buddha's own lips. The mother gives birth standing. The newborn stands on his own feet, takes seven steps, looks around, and declares that he is foremost in the world and that this is his last birth. Two streams of water, one cool and one warm, appear from the sky to bathe mother and child. That's the wonder the ladles repeat, and the flowers stand for the garden at Lumbini, where tradition places the birth. Now the turn. When Ananda finishes, the Buddha doesn't add a louder miracle. In paraphrase, he says: then remember this too as wonderful. For the one who has woken up, feelings are known as they arise, as they stay, and as they pass away. So are perceptions. So are thoughts. After all the marvels of the birth, the sutta ends on the plainest one: seeing clearly what is happening in one's own mind. That changes how the festival can look. The baby with one hand raised is where the story starts. A child's full attention on a ladle and a thin stream of tea is closer to where the sutta ends.
screen: `MONKS MARVELING AFTER THE MEAL.` · `ANANDA'S LIST OF BIRTH WONDERS.` · `TWO STREAMS OF WATER, COOL AND WARM.` · then, large: `FEELINGS KNOWN AS THEY ARISE AND PASS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: pour gently. If you have a cup of tea or water nearby, hold it. If not, picture one. Sit, and let the breath settle. Slowly, with full attention, pour a little water: over a plant, into a glass, into your own palm. Notice the sound, the weight, the way it moves. Pour as if over something new and fragile. Then set the cup down and rest your hands. Breathe, and stay a moment with how careful that was. The bell holds the time.
Flower festival. Hanamatsuri, when temples in Japan cover a small shrine in flowers and people pour sweet tea over the baby Buddha, remembering his birth in the garden. Today's word.
Your line: sweet tea. Today, make one cup of something for someone else, and pour it slowly, the way the children pour over the baby Buddha. Day one thousand fifty-four.

howItsDone: At Hanamatsuri, temples in Japan set up a small flower-covered shrine with a statue of the newborn Buddha, and visitors ladle sweet tea over it, and some take tea home to drink.

fork.setup: Ananda has just recited the wonders of the birth: seven steps, two streams of water from the sky. what does the Buddha add?
options: a greater miracle from the night of his awakening
feelings, perceptions and thoughts known as they arise, stay and pass
a promise of more wonders to come
fork.reveal: he tells Ananda to remember this too as wonderful: for the one who has woken up, feelings, perceptions and thoughts are known as they arise, stay and pass away.

original.note: Pali puppha: flower. the shrine's flowers stand for the garden where the Buddha was born.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty spring festival with tea.
what it means: a birth honored by bathing the baby Buddha, as the story says he was bathed.
what a scholar hears: Majjhima Nikaya 123, Ananda's list of birth wonders, closed by the Buddha's own: feelings known as they arise and pass.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 123 (Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta): the birth, seven steps, two streams of water, and the closing wonder of feelings known as they arise and pass

notes: MN 123 is paraphrased: newborn stands, takes seven steps (to the north in the Pali), surveys the quarters and declares he is foremost in the world and this is his last birth; two streams of water, cool and warm, appear from the sky. The 'seven steps' count is in the cited text. Confirm.
The one-hand-up, one-hand-down statue linked to the declaration: standard iconography (tenjo tenge yuiga dokuson); confirm.
Dragons (nine dragons in some tellings) pouring the water: given as 'East Asian tellings', no number. Confirm.
Amacha is brewed from leaves of a hydrangea variety; described only as 'leaves that come out naturally sweet'. Confirm.
No date is given for Hanamatsuri (commonly April 8).

Editor pass: removed 'the first thing done for the newborn was a bath' and the fork's 'first thing' framing, since in MN 123 deities receive the child before the streams of water; 'many temples' and 'often take some home' softened (claims rule); a garbled practice line smoothed.

Audit pass: hook and teach nearly repeated year one's 'Bathing the baby Buddha' (day 146: same shrine scene, seven steps, two streams, dragons, amacha, and the same two-streams myth). Rewritten: the hook now names the return, and the teach turns to MN 123's frame (monks marveling after the meal, Ananda reciting the wonders) and its ending, where the Buddha adds feelings, perceptions and thoughts known as they arise, remain and pass away. Dragons and amacha dropped (told in year one). Myth, fork, match and trapdoor updated. Confirm the paraphrase of MN 123's close.
